lead: Baltimore's rowhouses and thousands of vacant buildings make fire a block-by-block problem. SootMend helps homes and businesses across the city recover from fire, smoke and soot.
risk: rowhouse fires that spread to neighbors, fires in vacant buildings, and heating and electrical fires in old homes
why: More than four in ten Baltimore homes were built before 1940, most of them brick rowhouses that share walls and roof spaces. A fire in one home often damages the houses on both sides. Fires in vacant rowhouses are especially dangerous; a January 2022 vacant rowhouse fire on South Stricker Street killed three Baltimore firefighters.

Gas heats about six in ten homes, and some still use oil, which brings puff-back soot. Old wiring and space heaters add winter risk. Board-up after a fire keeps weather and trespassers out of damaged rowhouses.
problems: Highlandtown, Hampden, Canton and West Baltimore
tips: Board up and secure a damaged rowhouse quickly.
Report open vacant buildings to the city.
Have older wiring checked by a licensed electrician.
Install smoke alarms on every level.
insurance: Maryland requires home improvement contractors to be licensed by the Maryland Home Improvement Commission, which also runs a guaranty fund for some homeowner losses.
areas: SootMend works across Baltimore, including Canton, Fells Point, Federal Hill, Hampden, Roland Park, Mount Vernon, Charles Village and Highlandtown.

faq.q: What should I do if a vacant rowhouse next door burns in Baltimore?
faq.a: Make sure the fire department has cleared your home. Check the shared wall, roof and attic for hidden fire and water damage. Your homeowners policy usually covers your damage; document it and report it.
